passage:
Sunday, late
Binita cancelled on me again, the third Sunday in a row. Her message said "still fixing the thesis chapter, sorry sorry". I went over with momos anyway. Her room was dark except for the laptop, and she had those grey circles under her eyes. She showed me the chapter. It was good, really good. She'd spent two days on the spacing of one table. I didn't argue. I just said, "Let me read it like a rough draft that only has to be good enough. Only to see if it makes sense. Nothing else." She hesitated so long I thought she'd say no. Then she turned the laptop to me. I read it while she ate. I found one real typo. She laughed, fixed it and sent it to her guide at 11 p.m. Then she fell asleep on the sofa.
Tenzin

qa.q: How long had Binita spent on the spacing of one table?
qa.a: Two days.

qa.q: Why did Binita hesitate so long before turning the laptop around?
qa.a: Letting someone see the chapter meant risking that its flaws would be noticed, and after days of polishing, that felt frightening.

qa.q: Which choice by Tenzin helped Binita send the chapter?
qa.a: Offering to read it only as a good-enough draft, and staying while she ate, so checking felt safe and limited.

qa.q: What was it like for Binita to have Tenzin there?
qa.a: With company and one small typo found, the imperfection felt survivable, and she could finally send it and sleep.

grounding: A friend notices someone cancelling plans and losing sleep over tiny flaws, and offers to read it as a good-enough draft.

passage: Noa had booked a table at the ramen place near Umeda for Hiroshi's birthday, but at six he texted: "Sorry, can't. Still fixing the catalogue layout." It was his second cancellation that week. Noa got two portions to take away and climbed the stairs to his flat. Hiroshi opened the door in yesterday's shirt, eyes red. On his screen, the furniture catalogue looked finished to her. "The margins on page nine are off by a millimetre," he said. "And the grey is a bit too warm. I was up till four." Noa set the noodles on his desk. "Can I see it as a draft? Just a good-enough draft. We go through it together for thirty minutes, and whatever's left, you write down and send it anyway." He hesitated, then slid the laptop over. By eight they were eating, and the file was in his client's inbox.

Dear Chaitanya,

I didn't want to say this at the café, so I'm writing.

You've cancelled on us three Sundays in a row. When we did meet, you were checking your laptop under the table. You told me you'd slept four hours because the header on your grant application "looked wrong." I looked at it. It looked fine. You kept pointing to a line spacing I couldn't even see.

I'm worried. Not about the grant; about you.

Here's an offer. Send me the application tonight, as it is. I'll treat it as a draft that's already fine, not a final. I'll mark only the things that actually matter. Then you close the laptop and come to lunch on Sunday.

The grant will be fine. You're more important than the spacing.

Baljeet

qa.a: Three Sundays in a row.

qa.q: How does Baljeet feel about what's happening with Chaitanya?
qa.a: Baljeet feels worried, more about Chaitanya's lost sleep and cancelled plans than about the grant.

qa.a: It lets Chaitanya share imperfect work safely with a friend, which can make flaws feel survivable and let the work be finished.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya feel receiving this letter?

passage: So you want to know why Noor and I are closer now? It started with a wedding. Noor was designing the invitation card for her cousin, and for two weeks she disappeared. Missed our movie night. Missed my birthday dinner. When I went to her flat, she had forty versions of the same card on her screen, and her eyes were red. She'd been up till three because the gold border was one pixel thicker on the left. One pixel! I couldn't even see it. And I realised this wasn't about the card. She looked scared. So I sat down and said, "Show me the best one. We'll call it a good draft. I'll check it with you, and we send it tonight." She hesitated. Then she clicked one. We fixed two small things together. She sent it. Then she slept for eleven hours. That's how, and it's Ankita telling you.

Saturday. Jaya waited at the café for forty minutes before Vaibhav texted: "So sorry, portfolio still not right." It was the third cancelled plan that month. Jaya ate alone and felt a small, sour sting.

Tuesday. Jaya dropped by with food. Vaibhav's eyes were red. On the screen, he was zooming into a logo, nudging a curve. "Nobody would see that," Jaya said. "I would," he muttered. He admitted he had slept four hours a night since Friday.

Jaya sat down beside him. "Send it to me tonight as a rough draft. I'll look at it like a client, not a judge."

Thursday. Vaibhav sent it at nine with the subject line "good enough?" Jaya found two real fixes and wrote, "Rest is fine." He slept that night, and on Sunday he actually came to the café.

You think your manager will eat you alive over one slide, beta? Listen to your old Arnab mama. When I was twenty-five I shared a flat with Vinita, who did designs for a printing press. Clever girl, sharper than me.

That winter she stopped coming to our Sunday cricket and stopped eating dinner with us. I would wake at two and see her lamp still on, and her rubbing out a line she'd drawn ten times.

One night I asked to see it. It was a poster for a school fair. It was beautiful. She said the border was uneven. I said, "Vinita, show me the version you'd give if the press opened in one hour." She laughed, but she handed it over, and I told her the two things I'd really change.

She sent it the next morning. The school printed three hundred copies. Later she told me, "Arnab, you only looked, you didn't judge." That was all I did.

qa.a: Vinita's poster was for a school fair.

qa.q: What did young Arnab feel when he saw Vinita's lamp still on at two?
qa.a: Arnab felt worried for Vinita, noticing she had stopped cricket and dinners and was rubbing out the same line again and again.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it work?
qa.a: Arnab asking for the version Vinita would give if the press opened in one hour turned the poster into a deadline draft, so she could hand it over and hear only two real changes.

qa.a: Vinita felt he only looked and did not judge, which made showing the imperfect border feel safe enough to send it.

The power went out across the colony at eight, and Simran's grant proposal was due at midnight. Pradeep came up the stairs with a torch and found her on the balcony, laptop at eleven percent, rereading the budget table for the twentieth time.

"You cancelled my birthday dinner for this," Pradeep said gently. "Is it nearly done?"

"The table's fine. It's the wording. It sounds clumsy."

"Let me read it as a draft. Just one pass, then you send it before the battery dies."

She hesitated, then turned the screen. By torchlight Pradeep read aloud. Two sentences really were clumsy; they fixed them in five minutes. The rest was solid.

At nine percent Simran pressed submit. She sat back, shaking a little. "I haven't slept properly in a week," she said. Pradeep switched off the torch and they sat in the dark, listening to the generators hum.

qa.a: Simran's laptop was at nine percent when she pressed submit.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling when he found Simran on the balcony?
qa.a: Pradeep felt concerned and a little hurt, since she had cancelled his birthday dinner, but he spoke gently because he could see she was under strain.

qa.a: Pradeep offered one read-through as a draft; it found the two clumsy sentences quickly and showed the rest was solid, so she could submit.

passage:
I'm Sabina, and I share a flat with Kunal in Pune. In March I noticed he stopped coming to our Friday dinners with the neighbours. Then he stopped coming out of his room.
One night at two, I went to the kitchen for water and saw his light on. He was hunched over his first app, the one he'd been building for a year, fixing a button colour.
"It's almost ready," he said. "I just keep seeing things."
I remembered the week I spent redoing my own thesis cover, so I didn't lecture. I said, "Can I be your first user? Tomorrow at ten. I'll treat it like a rough draft. You tell me what's bothering you, and I'll tell you if I even notice."
He almost said no. Then he nodded.
The next morning I used it for twenty minutes. I noticed nothing about the button. He watched my face the whole time, and slowly his shoulders came down.

qa.q: How long had Kunal been building the app?
qa.a: He had been building it for a year.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling when seeing Kunal's light on at two?
qa.a: Sabina felt concerned and understanding, remembering having redone a thesis cover for a week, which is why Sabina chose not to lecture.

qa.q: Why was Sabina's offer to be the first user helpful?
qa.a: Treating the app as a rough draft and using it with Kunal showed him that others don't notice the tiny flaws, making imperfection feel survivable.

qa.q: How does Kunal seem to feel as Sabina uses the app?
qa.a: Kunal seems tense at first, watching Sabina's face, and then relieved, with his shoulders coming down.
